content:
The independent committee hearing for Wang Fuk Court has revealed that the management company "Cheung邦興業" (置邦興業) once compiled a file named "Units Authorising Wong Bik-kiu" (授權黃碧嬌的單位), showing that at the owners' meeting held on 11 December 2021 to appoint the consultant "Hung Ngai" (鴻毅), 131 proxy votes were related to Wong Bik-kiu's team, accounting for about 25% of all proxy votes that day. After obtaining the authorisation records, "集誌社" (Citizen News) discovered that the 131 proxy votes were authorised to 53 people, including Wong Bik-kiu; based on a tally of these 53 names, the number of proxy votes Wong Bik-kiu's "friendly" parties held that day amounted to 252, nearly half of the total. What is the background of this extensive network? Among them, five people share the same names as former Tai Wo Estate owners' corporation committee members, whose corporation was ousted in 2016 over a controversy involving exorbitant repair works; some of these former Tai Wo Estate committee members also showed up at the Wang Fuk Court owners' meeting in December 2021 in a "cross-estate" appearance. Records show that the consultant "Ho Hei" (浩熙), involved in the Tai Wo Estate repair dispute, had won the contract at a low price and had previously tendered for Wang Fuk Court projects; when "Ho Hei" served as consultant for King Tin Court in Sha Tin, the works were awarded to "Wang Yip" (宏業), and owners had filed a lawsuit alleging bid-rigging. The reporter contacted Wong Bik-kiu via text message, email and through a district councillor's office, but received no reply before deadline. Related reports: Tracking Wong Bik-kiu's proxy votes · 2 | 53 people obtained 131 proxy votes — Who are they? Some have backgrounds in DAB, New Association, etc. Tracking Wong Bik-kiu's proxy votes · 3 | After two owners passed away, their names appeared on the "Units Authorising Wong Bik-kiu" list — Families were unaware

The hearing revealed that Wang Fuk Court held an owners' meeting on 11 December 2021, with 131 proxy votes linked to Wong Bik-kiu's team; the agenda that day included appointing the works consultant "Hung Ngai" and a motion to remove the former owners' corporation. (Owners' corporation photo)

The hearing disclosed that Wong Bik-kiu initially admitted to having received only around 20 proxy votes, but the committee found a file from the management company "Hop On" (合安) titled "Units Authorising Wong Bik-kiu", documenting that she had 131 proxy votes at the 2021 meeting, accounting for about 25% of proxy votes that day. The majority of these 131 proxy votes were not made out to Wong Bik-kiu as the authorised representative; she later explained through her lawyer that the figure was a "joint tally" with her volunteer team, the incumbent corporation committee members and community friends, who together "assisted in handling" 131 votes, and that only around 20-odd specifically authorised her personally.

"集誌社" has obtained several sets of Wang Fuk Court owners' meeting proxy vote records, including proxy lists for the meetings on 25 January 2019 appointing "Hung Ngai" as Registered Inspector (RI), 11 December 2021 appointing "Hung Ngai" as consultant, 28 January 2024 appointing "Wang Yip" (宏業) as contractor, and 6 September 2024 appointing a new owners' corporation, as well as the "Units Authorising Wong Bik-kiu" file.

In December 2021, former Tai Wo Estate owners' corporation chairperson Tam Lai-ha (left), treasurer Shek Yuk-jan (front centre), committee members Ng Ling-lan (back centre) and Mok Shuk-jing (right) showed up at the Wang Fuk Court owners' meeting. That day, Mok Shuk-jing was seen holding a stack of papers, standing near the "Proxy Vote Registration Counter". (Photo provided by interviewee)

Former Tai Wo Estate corporation members embroiled in repair dispute show up at Wang Fuk Court meeting

The 131 proxy votes at the December 2021 owners' meeting involved 129 owners, with the first authorised representatives comprising 53 people including Wong Bik-kiu. Among them, "Tam Lai-ha", "Shek Yuk-jan", "Mok Shuk-jing", "Yiu Kam-sheung" and "Ng Ling-lan" each held 3 to 4 proxy votes, totalling 17 votes. These five people share the same names as former Tai Wo Estate owners' corporation committee members — Tam Lai-ha was the former chairperson, Shek Yuk-jan the former treasurer, and the remaining three were former committee members.

Former Tai Wo Estate mutual aid committee member A (pseudonym), concerned about repair and corporation disputes, went to the Wang Fuk Court owners' meeting venue in December 2021 to observe the situation. She recalled that upon arrival she noticed several former Tai Wo Estate corporation committee members, including Tam Lai-ha, Shek Yuk-jan, Mok Shuk-jing and Ng Ling-lan, were present. "I found it very strange at the time, as if they were the hosts — the entire venue had Wong Bik-kiu doing the greeting… It wouldn't be unusual if one or two came, but an entire team showed up… My instinct was it must have something to do with you people?" A provided photos from that day, pointing out that Mok Shuk-jing was holding a stack of papers and standing beside the "Proxy Vote Registration Counter", constantly making phone calls while "wandering around" and "queuing to collect voting papers".

Tai Wo Estate was embroiled in a 2016 controversy over exorbitant repair works involving alleged bid-rigging. The then-incumbent owners' corporation eventually retendered, and the project cost was slashed from HK$27 million to between HK$500,000 and HK$700,000. The corporation was subsequently ousted.

Speaking of the Tai Wo Estate bid-rigging controversy, A noted that Tai Wo residents had approached the Housing Bureau's ICU, which supervised the works, and learned that the government repair order only covered a small portion of the exterior walls of buildings where concrete spalling had occurred. However, the corporation decided, without consulting residents, to repair the entire exterior walls of all three blocks, and lobbied on the grounds that the estate maintenance fund had over HK$100 million and residents would not need to contribute; when they tried to understand the decision, residents were refused entry to meetings on the grounds that attendance was limited to five people.

Records show that the Tenants Purchase Scheme estate Tai Wo Estate was caught up in a 2016 dispute over inflated repair costs. Tam Lai-ha and Shek Yuk-jan were the then corporation chairperson and treasurer, while Yiu Kam-sheung, Mok Shuk-jing and Ng Ling-lan were committee members. The corporation hired the consultant "Ho Hei Construction Engineering Consultants" to conduct an external wall survey at a fee of around HK$150,000, and the quote for external wall repairs across the three blocks reached as high as HK$27 million, requiring each household to shoulder over HK$10,000. The project costs sparked bid-rigging allegations, and after residents pushed for a retender, the project cost was reduced to between HK$500,000 and HK$700,000. The former corporation was ousted the same year.

Tam Lai-ha (seventh from left) ran in the 2003 District Council elections under the Democratic Alliance for the Betterment and Progress of Hong Kong (DAB) banner and lost. She served as chairperson of the Tai Wo Estate owners' corporation from the early 2000s until being ousted in 2016. The photo shows a group shot at the 2015 Tai Po Rural Committee inauguration dinner; Wong Bik-kiu is second from left. (Facebook photo)

Former Tai Wo corporation chairperson was a DAB affiliate

Tam Lai-ha, the former Tai Wo corporation chairperson who appeared on the "Authorising Wong Bik-kiu" list and obtained proxy votes at Wang Fuk Court, has DAB connections. She ran on the party's ticket in the 2003 Tai Po District Council election and lost, while her party colleague Wong Bik-kiu won. In 2006, Tam Lai-ha was appointed as an added member of the Tai Po District Council Culture, Recreation and Sports Committee. During the September 2016 New Territories East by-election, she campaigned for DAB candidates Chan Hak-kan and Chow Ho-ting. Former committee member Mok Shuk-jing served alongside Wong Bik-kiu on the 2009 Tai Po District Fight Crime Committee, and became a specially invited director of the New Association in 2021; Yiu Kam-sheung is also a New Association Tai Po district director; Shek Yuk-jan and Ng Ling-lan are current members of the Tai Po Bunya constituency Care Team.

In addition to the December 2021 owners' meeting appointing "Hung Ngai", "Shek Yuk-jan" and "Ng Ling-lan" each received one proxy vote at the September 2024 owners' meeting that appointed the new corporation, when "Wong Chun-yau" (黃進有) was also listed as another authorised representative. Records show that "Wong Chun-yau" co-founded "Lok Kwan Volunteer Alliance" (樂群義工聯盟) with Wong Bik-kiu.

The reporter contacted Wong Bik-kiu via text message, email and through a district councillor's office, but received no reply before deadline.

Wong Bik-kiu founded "Lok Kwan Volunteer Alliance" (樂群義工聯盟) with Wong Chun-yau (left in photo) and Ting Kit-mui (right in photo). On the "Units Authorising Wong Bik-kiu" list, there are authorised persons sharing the same names, as well as persons of the same name connected to "Lok Kwan Volunteers" (樂群義工). (Facebook photo)

Tai Wo Estate consultant had tendered for Wang Fuk Court; King Tin Court project it oversaw was awarded to Wang Yip

"Ho Hei" (浩熙), which charged Tai Wo Estate a rock-bottom consultancy price, was founded by Wong Siu-cheung, who also tendered for Wang Fuk Court projects. In January 2019, "Ho Hei" tendered for the Wang Fuk Court Registered Inspector (RI) position at HK$700,000, but lost out to "Hung Ngai"'s HK$220,000 bid.

By 2021, "Tai Tei Construction Consultants Limited" (大地建築顧問有限公司), for which Wong Siu-cheung had served as director, tendered for the Wang Fuk Court consultancy at HK$400,000, slightly above "Hung Ngai"'s HK$300,000 and failing to win; "Fast Profit Architectural Engineering Consultants Limited" (快利達建築工程顧問有限公司) tendered at HK$280,000 for the same role but was likewise unsuccessful. Wong Siu-cheung became a director of "Fast Profit" the following year.

Court documents show that in 2009, King Tin Court in Sha Tin engaged "Ho Hei" as project consultant; following the 2011 tender, "Wang Yip" (宏業) was appointed contractor for works valued at HK$91 million. In 2012, owners filed a lawsuit alleging bid-rigging and seeking to overturn the contract, but lost.

"Ho Hei", which won the Tai Wo Estate repair consultancy at a low price in 2016, later tendered for the Wang Fuk Court Registered Inspector role, and related companies also tendered for the consultancy — all bids exceeded "Hung Ngai"'s and failed to win.

Wong Siu-cheung and Wong Siu-keung, who was previously involved in the Sha Tin Villa Esplanada bid-rigging case, are also believed to be related parties. During the trial of the HK$260 million bid-rigging case at Sha Tin Villa Esplanada, it was revealed that Wong Siu-cheung, a director of "Universal Housing" (環球屋宇), paid "tea money" and introduction fees to corporation members and works subcontractors, and arranged for shadow companies to bid so that "Universal Housing" would win the contract; in 2023, Wong Siu-cheung was arrested in connection with an alleged HK$160 million bid-rigging case at Discovery Bay. Company searches show that one of Wong Siu-cheung's former construction companies, which has since been dissolved, once shared the same registered address used by Wong Siu-keung.
